1:1.t: "My former book": the Gospel of Luke (Luke 1:3).

1:3.t: "Suffering": the KJV's "passion". "Convincing proofs": the KJV's "infallible proofs".

1:12.t: "A Sabbath day's walk": about one kilometer, the distance a Jew was allowed to travel on the Sabbath.

1:13.t: "Simon the Zealot": the KJV's "Simon Zelotes". "Judas the brother of James": see Luke 6:16.

1:18.t: Matthew 27:3-8 tells of Judas's death differently: the priests bought the field with his money, and he hanged himself. The two accounts may describe different sides of the same events. "Akeldama": the KJV's "Aceldama", Aramaic for "field of blood".

1:20.t: Quotations of Psalm 69:25 and 109:8. "Place of leadership": the KJV's "bishoprick"; Greek episkope, the office of overseer.

1:26.t: Casting lots was a recognized way of seeking God's choice (Proverbs 16:33). It is not used again in the New Testament after the Spirit was given.

2:1.t: Pentecost, the Festival of Weeks, came fifty days after Passover (Leviticus 23:15-21). It celebrated the wheat harvest and, in Jewish tradition, the giving of the law at Sinai.

2:9.t: The list moves roughly from east to west across the Jewish dispersion. "Asia" is the Roman province in western Asia Minor (now Turkey).

2:15.t: "Nine in the morning": the KJV's "the third hour of the day".

3:1.t: "At three in the afternoon": the KJV's "the ninth hour", the time of the evening sacrifice and prayer.

3:2.t: The Beautiful Gate was probably the bronze Nicanor Gate on the east side of the temple courts.

4:1.t: "The captain of the temple guard": the officer in charge of the temple police, second in rank to the high priest.

4:6.t: Annas was still called high priest after his removal from office; see Luke 3:2.

4:13.t: "Unschooled, ordinary men": the KJV's "unlearned and ignorant men", meaning without formal training in the law, not unintelligent.
"Courage" (Greek parresia): the KJV's "boldness", frank, open, fearless speech. It is a key word in Acts (4:29, 4:31, 28:31).

4:25.t: "Your servant David": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts read "our father David, Your servant, by the Holy Spirit". The quotation is Psalm 2:1-2.

4:36.t: "Joses": the KJV's reading; many manuscripts read "Joseph". "Son of encouragement": the KJV's "the son of consolation"; Greek paraklesis, related to parakletos (see John 14:16).

5:21.t: "The Sanhedrin, the full assembly of the elders of Israel": the KJV's "the council ... and all the senate of the children of Israel".

5:30.t: "On a tree": the KJV's reading. The cross is called a tree, recalling Deuteronomy 21:22-23 (compare Galatians 3:13).

5:34.t: Gamaliel was the most respected rabbi of his day and Paul's teacher (22:3).

5:36.t: Theudas is otherwise unknown from this time; the historian Josephus mentions a later rebel of that name. Judas the Galilean led a revolt against the Roman census of AD 6.

6:1.t: "Hellenistic Jews ... Hebraic Jews": the KJV's "Grecians ... Hebrews", Greek-speaking Jews from outside the land and Aramaic-speaking Jews of Judea.

6:5.t: "A convert to Judaism": the KJV's "a proselyte".

6:9.t: "The Synagogue of the Freedmen": the KJV's "the synagogue of the Libertines", Jews who had been freed from slavery, or their descendants. Cilicia was Paul's home province (22:3).

7:6.t: A quotation of Genesis 15:13-14, with Exodus 3:12.

7:14.t: "Seventy-five": the Greek Old Testament of Genesis 46:27 and Exodus 1:5; the Hebrew has seventy.

7:16.t: "Shechem ... Hamor": the KJV's "Sychem ... Emmor". Genesis 23 says Abraham bought a cave at Hebron, and Genesis 33:19 that Jacob bought land at Shechem from Hamor's sons. Stephen's summary combines the two.

7:37.t: A quotation of Deuteronomy 18:15. "Him you shall hear": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts do not have these words.

7:42.t: A quotation of Amos 5:25-27 from the Greek. "Molech": the KJV's "Moloch". "Rephan": the KJV's "Remphan", perhaps a name for the planet Saturn.

7:45.t: "Joshua": the KJV's "Jesus", the Greek form of the name Joshua.

8:5.t: "The city of Samaria": the KJV's reading; some manuscripts read "a city of Samaria".

8:9.t: Simon is known in early Christian writings as Simon Magus, "the magician".

8:26.t: "Which is desert": either the road or the old city of Gaza.

8:27.t: "Kandake": the KJV's "Candace", a royal title of the queen mother of Ethiopia (ancient Nubia, south of Egypt), not a personal name. A eunuch could not fully join the assembly of Israel (Deuteronomy 23:1), but Isaiah 56:3-5 promised them a place.

8:32.t: A quotation of Isaiah 53:7-8 from the Greek.

8:37.t: The KJV includes this verse; many early manuscripts do not have it.

8:40.t: Azotus is the Old Testament Ashdod.

9:2.t: "The Way": an early name for the followers of Jesus (19:9, 19:23, 24:14).

9:5.t: "It is hard for you to kick against the goads. Trembling and astonished, he asked, 'Lord, what do You want me to do?' The Lord said to him": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts do not have these words here (compare 26:14, 22:10). A goad was a pointed stick for driving oxen; kicking against it only hurt the animal.

9:7.t: Compare 22:9: the companions heard a sound but did not understand the words.

9:11.t: Tarsus was the capital of Cilicia, a center of learning.

9:23.t: Paul spent some of this time in Arabia (Galatians 1:17-18).

9:35.t: Sharon is the coastal plain north of Joppa.

9:43.t: Tanners handled dead animals and were considered ceremonially unclean; Peter's stay there prepares for chapter 10.

10:1.t: Caesarea, on the coast, was the Roman capital of Judea. "Italian Regiment": the KJV's "the Italian band", a cohort of about six hundred soldiers.

10:2.t: "God-fearing": a term for Gentiles who worshiped the God of Israel and kept many Jewish customs without becoming full converts.

10:3.t: "Three in the afternoon": the KJV's "the ninth hour", a set time of prayer (3:1).

10:30.t: "Three in the afternoon": the KJV's "the ninth hour", a set time of prayer (3:1).

10:9.t: "About noon": the KJV's "about the sixth hour". Flat roofs were used as quiet places.

10:14.t: The law of Moses forbade Israel to eat certain animals (Leviticus 11).

10:25.t: "Worshiped him": the Greek proskuneo, to bow down. See Matthew 2:2. Peter refuses such honor.

10:28.t: Jewish tradition, not the law of Moses itself, forbade close contact with Gentiles.

11:19.t: Phoenicia was the coastal region of Tyre and Sidon. Antioch in Syria was the third largest city of the Roman Empire.

11:20.t: "The Hellenistic Jews": the KJV's "the Grecians"; many manuscripts read "the Greeks", meaning Gentiles, which fits the context of a new outreach.

11:28.t: Claudius reigned AD 41-54; there were several famines during his reign.

12:1.t: King Herod: Herod Agrippa I, grandson of Herod the Great, king of Judea AD 41-44.

12:2.t: James son of Zebedee, the first of the Twelve to be martyred.

12:4.t: "Four squads of four soldiers": the KJV's "four quaternions", one squad for each watch of the night. "The Passover": the KJV's "Easter"; Greek pascha, the Passover festival.

12:12.t: John Mark later wrote the Gospel of Mark.

12:15.t: "His angel": many Jews believed each person had a guardian angel (compare Matthew 18:10).

12:17.t: James is the brother of Jesus, who became the leader of the Jerusalem church (15:13, Galatians 1:19).

12:20.t: "Blastus, a trusted personal servant": the KJV's "the king's chamberlain".

12:23.t: The historian Josephus also tells of Herod Agrippa's sudden death at Caesarea in AD 44.

13:1.t: Herod the tetrarch: Herod Antipas. "Niger" is Latin for "dark" or "black".

13:7.t: "Proconsul": the KJV's "deputy", the governor of a Roman province under the Senate.

13:9.t: Saul is his Hebrew name; Paul (Paulus) his Roman name. From here on Luke calls him Paul.

13:14.t: "Pisidian Antioch": a different city from Antioch in Syria.

13:15.t: "Leaders of the synagogue": the KJV's "the rulers of the synagogue".

13:18.t: "Endured their conduct": the KJV's reading; some manuscripts read "cared for them".

13:20.t: "After this, He gave them judges for about 450 years": the KJV's reading. Many early manuscripts read "All this took about 450 years. After this, He gave them judges", counting from the time in Egypt to the conquest.

13:41.t: A quotation of Habakkuk 1:5 from the Greek.

14:6.t: Lystra and Derbe were towns in Lycaonia, a region in the Roman province of Galatia. Timothy came from Lystra (16:1).

14:12.t: "Zeus ... Hermes": the KJV's "Jupiter ... Mercurius", the Roman names of the same gods. Hermes was the messenger of the gods. A local legend told of Zeus and Hermes visiting the region in human form.

14:14.t: Tearing one's clothes was a sign of horror at blasphemy.

14:15.t: "We too are only human, like you": the KJV's "We also are men of like passions with you".

15:13.t: James, the brother of Jesus; see 12:17.

15:14.t: "Simon": the KJV's "Simeon", the Hebrew form of Peter's name.

15:16.t: A quotation of Amos 9:11-12 from the Greek.

15:18.t: "All His works are known to God from the beginning of the world": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts read "things known from long ago", as the end of the quotation.

15:20.t: These requirements helped Jewish and Gentile believers share meals and fellowship. Several echo the laws for foreigners living in Israel (Leviticus 17-18).

15:29.t: These requirements helped Jewish and Gentile believers share meals and fellowship. Several echo the laws for foreigners living in Israel (Leviticus 17-18).

15:22.t: "Barsabbas": the KJV's "Barsabas". Silas is called Silvanus in Paul's letters.

15:23.t: "Syria and Cilicia": formed one Roman province at this time.

15:34.t: The KJV includes this verse; many early manuscripts do not have it.

16:3.t: Paul circumcised Timothy, whose mother was Jewish, so that his work among Jews would not be hindered; this was not a requirement for salvation (compare Galatians 2:3).

16:10.t: Here Luke begins to say "we", showing that he joined Paul at Troas. The "we" passages continue in 20:5-21:18 and 27:1-28:16.

16:12.t: A Roman colony was a city whose citizens had the rights of Roman citizens.

16:13.t: Philippi apparently had too few Jewish men to form a synagogue (ten were required), so the women met for prayer by the river.

16:14.t: Thyatira was famous for its purple dye, a luxury product.

16:16.t: "A spirit by which she predicted the future": the KJV's "a spirit of divination"; the Greek says "a spirit of Python", the serpent associated with the oracle at Delphi.

16:35.t: "Officers": the KJV's "serjeants", Greek rhabdouchoi, "rod-bearers", the attendants who carried out the magistrates' orders.

16:37.t: It was illegal to beat or imprison a Roman citizen without a trial.

17:1.t: Thessalonica was the capital of Macedonia. Paul later wrote two letters to the church there.

17:18.t: Epicureans taught that the gods took no interest in human affairs and that the aim of life was a tranquil pleasure. Stoics taught that reason ordered the universe and that the wise person lived in harmony with it. "Babbler": Greek spermologos, "seed-picker", like a bird picking up scraps, someone with borrowed ideas.

17:19.t: The Areopagus ("hill of Ares", the KJV's "Mars' hill", Mars being the Roman name of Ares) was both a hill near the Acropolis and the ancient council that met there.

17:26.t: "From one blood": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts read "from one man".

17:28.t: The first saying is attributed to the Cretan poet Epimenides; the second is from the Cilician poet Aratus.

17:34.t: "A member of the Areopagus": the KJV's "the Areopagite".

18:2.t: Claudius expelled the Jews from Rome in about AD 49, apparently after disputes about Christ.

18:5.t: "Compelled by the Spirit": the KJV's "pressed in the spirit"; many early manuscripts read "devoted himself entirely to the word".

18:6.t: Shaking out one's clothes was a sign of refusing any further responsibility (compare 13:51, Ezekiel 33:4).

18:12.t: "Proconsul": see 13:7. Gallio was proconsul of Achaia in AD 51-52, which helps date Paul's stay in Corinth. Achaia was the Roman province of southern Greece.

18:18.t: Cenchreae was the eastern port of Corinth. Cutting the hair marked the end of a Nazirite-type vow (Numbers 6:18).

18:21.t: "I must by all means keep this coming festival in Jerusalem": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts do not have these words.

19:1.t: "Through the interior": the KJV's "the upper coasts", the highland route.

19:9.t: "The lecture hall of Tyrannus": the KJV's "the school of one Tyrannus".

19:19.t: "Fifty thousand pieces of silver": probably drachmas, each about a day's wage.

19:24.t: "Artemis": the KJV's "Diana", the Roman name. The temple of Artemis at Ephesus was one of the seven wonders of the ancient world.

19:29.t: The theater at Ephesus held about 25,000 people.

19:31.t: "Officials of the province": the KJV's "the chief of Asia", Asiarchs, wealthy citizens who led the civic cult of the province.

19:35.t: "City clerk": the KJV's "townclerk", the chief local official. "Which fell from heaven": the KJV's "which fell down from Jupiter", probably a meteorite.

19:37.t: "Robbed temples": the KJV's "robbers of churches"; Greek hierosylous, temple robbers.

20:2.t: "Greece": Achaia. Paul probably wrote Romans during these three months in Corinth.

20:16.t: Paul hoped to bring the collection for the poor in Jerusalem (Romans 15:25-28, 1 Corinthians 16:1-4).

20:28.t: "The church of God, which He bought with His own blood": the KJV's reading. Some manuscripts read "the church of the Lord". The Greek can also mean "with the blood of His own [Son]".

"Overseers" (Greek episkopoi): the KJV's "overseers", the word later translated "bishops". Here the same men are called elders (20:17); in the New Testament the two titles describe the same leaders. "Be shepherds" (Greek poimainein): the KJV's "to feed", to tend as a shepherd; see John 21:16.

20:35.t: These words of Jesus are not recorded in the Gospels.

21:7.t: Ptolemais is the Old Testament Akko, north of Mount Carmel.

21:8.t: Philip was one of the Seven chosen in 6:5; see also 8:5-40.

21:24.t: Paying the expenses of a Nazirite's offerings was considered a pious act (Numbers 6:13-21).

21:28.t: A stone barrier in the temple warned Gentiles, on pain of death, not to enter the inner courts.

21:31.t: "The commander of the Roman troops": the KJV's "the chief captain of the band", a tribune commanding a cohort of about a thousand soldiers. His name is Claudius Lysias (23:26).

21:34.t: "The barracks": the KJV's "the castle", the Antonia Fortress, overlooking the temple courts.

21:38.t: The historian Josephus describes this Egyptian false prophet, who led a revolt about AD 54. "Terrorists": the KJV's "murderers"; Greek sikarioi, "dagger men", assassins who carried short daggers.

21:40.t: "Aramaic": the KJV's "the Hebrew tongue". See John 19:13.

22:2.t: "Aramaic": the KJV's "the Hebrew tongue". See John 19:13.

22:3.t: "I studied under Gamaliel": the KJV's "at the feet of Gamaliel", the position of a student. See 5:34.

22:5.t: "The Council": the KJV's "all the estate of the elders", the Sanhedrin.

22:9.t: "And were afraid": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts do not have these words. "Did not hear the voice": the Greek akouo can mean "hear" or "understand". Compare 9:7.

22:25.t: Flogging was used to extract confessions from non-citizens. See 16:37.

22:28.t: Citizenship could be bought, often through bribes. Paul inherited his.

23:2.t: Ananias son of Nedebaeus was high priest about AD 47-59, known for greed and violence.

23:3.t: "Whitewashed wall": a hypocrite, clean on the outside (compare Matthew 23:27, Ezekiel 13:10-15).

23:23.t: "Nine tonight": the KJV's "the third hour of the night".

23:24.t: Antonius Felix was governor of Judea about AD 52-59.

23:31.t: Antipatris was about 60 kilometers from Jerusalem, on the road to Caesarea.

23:35.t: "Herod's palace": the KJV's "Herod's judgment hall", the palace built by Herod the Great, now the governor's residence.

24:1.t: "A lawyer": the KJV's "a certain orator", a professional advocate.

24:6.t: "And would have judged him according to our law. But the commander Lysias came ... ordering his accusers to come before you": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts do not have these words.

24:24.t: Drusilla was a daughter of Herod Agrippa I (12:1). "Christ": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts read "Christ Jesus".

24:27.t: Porcius Festus succeeded Felix about AD 59.

25:11.t: A Roman citizen could appeal to the emperor, at this time Nero.

25:13.t: King Agrippa: Herod Agrippa II, son of Herod Agrippa I (12:1), ruler of territories north and east of Galilee. Bernice was his sister.

25:21.t: "The Emperor": the KJV's "Augustus", a title of the emperor, Greek sebastos, "revered one".

25:25.t: "The Emperor": the KJV's "Augustus", a title of the emperor, Greek sebastos, "revered one".

25:26.t: "His Majesty": the KJV's "my lord", Greek kyrios, a title given to the emperor.

26:14.t: "Aramaic": the KJV's "the Hebrew tongue". See John 19:13. "Kick against the goads": see 9:5.

27:2.t: Adramyttium was a port in the province of Asia, southeast of Troas.

27:9.t: "The Day of Atonement": the KJV's "the fast", in late September or October. After mid-September sailing in the Mediterranean became dangerous, and after mid-November it stopped for the winter.

27:14.t: "Euroclydon": the KJV's reading, the "east-northeast wind"; many early manuscripts read "Euraquilo", the northeaster.

27:16.t: "Clauda": the KJV's reading; some manuscripts read "Cauda".

27:17.t: "The quicksands": the KJV's reading; Greek Syrtis, the dangerous shoals off the coast of North Africa.

27:27.t: "The Adriatic Sea": the KJV's "Adria", which then meant the central Mediterranean between Greece, Italy and Africa.

27:28.t: "About 36 meters ... about 27 meters": the KJV's "twenty fathoms ... fifteen fathoms".

28:2.t: "The islanders": the KJV's "the barbarous people", meaning non-Greek-speaking people, not savages.

28:4.t: "The goddess Justice": the KJV's "vengeance"; Greek Dike, the goddess of justice.

28:11.t: Castor and Pollux, sons of Zeus, were the patron gods of sailors.

28:13.t: Puteoli, near Naples, was the main port for grain ships from Alexandria.

28:15.t: The Forum of Appius was about 70 kilometers from Rome, the Three Taverns about 50.

28:16.t: "The centurion handed the prisoners over to the captain of the guard": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts do not have these words.

28:26.t: A quotation of Isaiah 6:9-10 from the Greek.

28:29.t: The KJV includes this verse; many early manuscripts do not have it.

28:30.t: Paul probably wrote Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians and Philemon during this imprisonment. Early tradition says he was released, traveled further, and was later martyred in Rome under Nero.

1:8.t: "Witnesses" (Greek martys): those who testify to what they have seen. The word later came to mean "martyr", one who bears witness by dying. Acts follows the gospel's spread from Jerusalem to Judea and Samaria (chapters 1-12) and on to the ends of the earth (chapters 13-28).

2:3.t: "Tongues" (Greek glossa): both the tongue and a language. The "tongues of fire" and "other tongues" are the same word. Here they were real languages the hearers understood (2:6-11), the reverse of Babel's confusion (Genesis 11:1-9).

2:23.t: "Deliberate plan and foreknowledge" (Greek horismene boule kai prognosis): Jesus' death was God's purpose, yet those who carried it out were responsible.

2:27.t: "Hades": the KJV's "hell". See Matthew 11:23. Here it means the grave, the realm of the dead.

2:31.t: "Hades": the KJV's "hell". See Matthew 11:23. Here it means the grave, the realm of the dead.

2:38.t: "Repent and be baptized ... for the forgiveness of your sins" (Greek eis aphesin): Christians understand the link between baptism and forgiveness differently: as the means by which forgiveness is given, or as the outward sign of a forgiveness received through faith and repentance.

2:42.t: "Fellowship" (Greek koinonia): sharing in common, partnership, participation. It includes sharing possessions (2:44) and life together in Christ (1 John 1:3).

3:13.t: "Servant" (Greek pais): the KJV's "Son" in chapter 3 and "child" in chapter 4. Pais can mean child, son or servant. Here it echoes the Servant of the LORD in Isaiah 42:1 and 52:13-53:12, who suffers and is glorified.

3:26.t: "Servant" (Greek pais): the KJV's "Son" in chapter 3 and "child" in chapter 4. Pais can mean child, son or servant. Here it echoes the Servant of the LORD in Isaiah 42:1 and 52:13-53:12, who suffers and is glorified.

4:27.t: "Servant" (Greek pais): the KJV's "Son" in chapter 3 and "child" in chapter 4. Pais can mean child, son or servant. Here it echoes the Servant of the LORD in Isaiah 42:1 and 52:13-53:12, who suffers and is glorified.

4:30.t: "Servant" (Greek pais): the KJV's "Son" in chapter 3 and "child" in chapter 4. Pais can mean child, son or servant. Here it echoes the Servant of the LORD in Isaiah 42:1 and 52:13-53:12, who suffers and is glorified.

3:15.t: "Author of life" (Greek archegos): the KJV's "Prince of life". Archegos means leader, founder, pioneer, the one who goes first and opens the way (5:31, Hebrews 2:10, 12:2).

3:19.t: "Turn to God" (Greek epistrepsate): the KJV's "be converted". Repentance is a change of mind; turning is a change of direction.

3:21.t: "Restore everything" (Greek apokatastasis panton): the KJV's "restitution of all things", the renewal of creation promised by the prophets.

4:12.t: "Salvation" (Greek soteria): the same word means healing and rescue. The lame man's healing (sozo, 4:9) points to the salvation found only in Jesus.

6:2.t: "Wait on tables ... ministry of the word" (Greek diakonein ... diakonia): the same word, "service", is used for both. Serving food and serving the word are both ministry. The Seven are often seen as the first deacons (diakonoi), though Acts does not call them that.

7:38.t: "Assembly" (Greek ekklesia): the KJV's "church". Israel in the wilderness was God's gathered people; see Matthew 16:18. "Living words" (Greek logia zonta): the KJV's "the lively oracles", the life-giving words of God's law.

7:56.t: "Standing at the right hand of God": elsewhere Jesus is seated there (Psalm 110:1, Hebrews 1:3). Many see Him standing to welcome His first martyr, or as a witness rising in his defense.

7:60.t: "Fell asleep" (Greek ekoimethe): the New Testament often speaks of believers' death as sleep (1 Thessalonians 4:13-14), because they will be raised.

9:4.t: "Why do you persecute Me?": Jesus so identifies with His followers that to persecute them is to persecute Him (compare Matthew 25:40).

9:13.t: "Holy people" (Greek hagioi): the KJV's "saints". In the New Testament, all believers are "saints", set apart for God, not only a few exceptional people.

9:15.t: "Instrument" (Greek skeuos): the KJV's "vessel", a tool or container chosen for a purpose.

9:31.t: "Encouraged" (Greek paraklesis): the KJV's "comfort". See 4:36 and John 14:16.

10:34.t: "God does not show favoritism" (Greek prosopolemptes): the KJV's "God is no respecter of persons". Literally "a receiver of faces", one who judges by outward appearance or status (Deuteronomy 10:17).

10:44.t: The Spirit came on the Gentiles before they were baptized, showing that God accepted them as they were, without circumcision.

11:18.t: "Repentance that leads to life": the KJV's "repentance unto life". Repentance itself is God's gift.

11:26.t: "Christians" (Greek Christianoi): "Christ's people", "followers of Christ". The name was probably given by outsiders. It appears only three times in the New Testament (here, 26:28, 1 Peter 4:16).

13:2.t: "Worshiping" (Greek leitourgounton): the KJV's "ministered", priestly service; the source of the English word "liturgy".

13:34.t: "The holy and sure blessings promised to David" (Greek ta hosia David ta pista): the KJV's "the sure mercies of David", quoting Isaiah 55:3. The Hebrew there is hasdei David, God's steadfast love (hesed) promised to David. See Psalm 89:1-4.

13:39.t: "Justified" (Greek dikaioo): see Matthew 12:37. Paul's first recorded sermon already points to the teaching of Romans and Galatians.

13:48.t: "Appointed for eternal life" (Greek tetagmenoi): "arranged, set in order". Readers understand this as God's choosing, or as those who had set themselves toward eternal life. The grammar more naturally reads as God's appointing.

14:22.t: "Hardships" (Greek thlipsis): see John 16:33. Suffering is the normal path of discipleship.

14:23.t: "Elders" (Greek presbyteroi): the leaders of a local church, from the Jewish synagogue pattern. "Appointed" (Greek cheirotonesantes): literally "stretched out the hand", a word that could mean appointing or electing.

15:10.t: "Yoke": see Matthew 11:29-30. Peter means the burden of earning salvation by keeping the whole law.

15:11.t: "Grace" (Greek charis): God's free, undeserved favor. Peter reverses what the Pharisees expected: Jews are saved the same way as Gentiles, not the other way around.

16:30.t: "Saved" (Greek sozo): see Matthew 9:22. "You and your household": the promise is for each member who believes, as the whole household then did (16:34).

17:11.t: "More noble" (Greek eugenesteroi): open-minded, of better character. They tested Paul's teaching by the Scriptures.

17:22.t: "Very religious" (Greek deisidaimonesterous): the KJV's "too superstitious". The word can mean devout or superstitious; Paul likely uses it tactfully as a compliment that opens his speech.

17:30.t: "Overlooked" (Greek hyperidon): the KJV's "winked at", meaning that God did not yet bring judgment, not that He approved.

19:2.t: These disciples had received only John's baptism and had not heard of the coming of the Spirit. Christians understand this event differently: as a second experience after believing, or as these disciples' first full hearing of the gospel of Jesus.

19:32.t: "Assembly" (Greek ekklesia): the same word that means "church" (see Matthew 16:18), here a civic gathering of citizens.

19:39.t: "Assembly" (Greek ekklesia): the same word that means "church" (see Matthew 16:18), here a civic gathering of citizens.

19:41.t: "Assembly" (Greek ekklesia): the same word that means "church" (see Matthew 16:18), here a civic gathering of citizens.

20:24.t: "Finish the race" (Greek teleioso ton dromon): the KJV's "finish my course". Paul often pictures the Christian life as a race (1 Corinthians 9:24-27, 2 Timothy 4:7).

21:13.t: "For the name of the Lord Jesus": Paul's readiness echoes Jesus' own setting His face toward Jerusalem (Luke 9:51).

22:16.t: "Wash your sins away" (Greek apolousai): baptism is the outward washing that pictures, and for many Christians conveys, the inward cleansing received by calling on the Lord's name. See 2:38.

23:1.t: "Conscience" (Greek syneidesis): the inner awareness of right and wrong before God. Paul uses the word often in his letters (Romans 2:15, 1 Corinthians 8:7-12).

24:16.t: "Conscience" (Greek syneidesis): the inner awareness of right and wrong before God. Paul uses the word often in his letters (Romans 2:15, 1 Corinthians 8:7-12).

24:14.t: "Sect" (Greek hairesis): the KJV's "heresy". The word first meant a party or school of thought (5:17, 15:5, 24:5); only later did "heresy" come to mean false teaching.

24:25.t: "Self-control" (Greek enkrateia): the KJV's "temperance", mastery over one's desires. Felix and Drusilla's marriage had been an adulterous scandal.

26:18.t: "Sanctified" (Greek hegiasmenois): set apart as God's own. See John 17:17.

26:28.t: "You almost persuade me to be a Christian" (Greek en oligo me peitheis Christianon poiesai): the KJV's reading. The Greek is difficult and may be ironic: "In such a short time do you think you can persuade me to be a Christian?" Paul's reply (26:29) plays on "in a short time" or "almost".

27:24.t: "Has graciously given you" (Greek kecharistai): from charis, grace, a gift freely given.

28:31.t: "Boldness" (Greek parresia): see 4:13. "Without hindrance" (Greek akolytos): the last word of Acts in Greek. The gospel has reached the heart of the empire, and it goes on unhindered.
